text: Every year, pests destroy up to forty percent of the world's crops. And as the climate warms, many of them breed faster. So farmers spray more often, pay more, and their soil grows poorer.

text: Field Shift turns NASA's view of the Earth into advice for one field. Here is how it works, on a pea field in the Huaral valley, in Peru.
asr: Field Shift turns NASA's view of the Earth into advice for one field. Here is how it works, on a pea field in the Huaral valley, in Peru.

text: Start with your field. Use your GPS, search a place, or open the example site. Drop a point, or draw the outline. Field Shift measures the area for you.
asr: Start with your field. Use your GPS, search a place, or open the example site. Drop a point, or draw the outline. Field Shift measures the area for you.

text: Then tell it what you would tell your agronomist. What grows now, what grew before, how you water. If you don't know, say so. Send photos at full resolution, or simply talk. It asks for what is missing, like a closer look at the underside of a leaf.

text: Meanwhile, NASA data reads your field. Forty years of NASA POWER weather show these weeks running five degrees warmer than normal. NASA's SMAP satellite measures soil moisture. Sentinel-2 maps crop vigor, ten meters per pixel. Every reading shows its source, its date, and whether it describes your field or the whole region.

text: Then the readings become a plan. Prevention ranks the pests likely on your field, with NASA's GEOS-FP weather forecast. Organic care names the natural enemies to protect, like lady beetles and parasitoid wasps, and beneficial fungi such as Trichoderma. Rotation compares your current rotation with two alternatives, for soil health, water and pest cycles. And you can ask: what if I grow avocado? It is scored the same way.
